messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Chaplain
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Crowding: Crowded places, Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi, a 34-year-old South Eastern Asian man who worked as a chaplain, came to therapy after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed around a single night. He had been walking home after an evening visit when two men cornered him near a convenience store, one coming close enough that Ravi could hear the man’s heavy breathing before the first demand was made. The robbery was quick and humiliating, but what stayed with Ravi was not just the loss of his wallet and phone; it was the sense of being watched, pinned, and overpowered while strangers moved around him on the street without intervening. In the weeks that followed, he began to feel that people connected to that event were dangerous in a way he could not easily explain, and crowds became intolerable. At the grocery store, in the chapel foyer after services, even on the train platform, he scanned faces and bodies for anyone who reminded him of the men who took his belongings. Heavy breathing in a crowded space would make his chest tighten immediately, because it pulled him back to the robbery before he had time to think.

When Ravi described the event, it came back to him mostly in pictures: the fluorescent spill of light on wet pavement, the angle of one man’s shoulders, the other man’s hand reaching into his coat. He said he could still sometimes smell the sour sweat and stale smoke that hung in the air that night, and those sensations arrived with a surge of intense rage that startled him with its force. That rage did not stay neatly in the memory. It fed his belief that something about him had made the robbery possible, that the sort of person he was invited harm, and that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation. He was ashamed of how quickly he had frozen, ashamed that as a chaplain—someone who sat with fear and suffering in others—he had not somehow protected himself. The more he replayed the event in fragments of image and smell, the more certain he became that he had been marked as an easy target, and that he could not stop bad things from happening to him.

Those conclusions made his world feel less safe and his attention more locked onto threat. Ravi started avoiding places where people moved close together, especially the busier parts of downtown near his church and the crowded cafés where he used to meet parishioners. He declined hospital visits that required him to take packed elevators or walk through busy lobbies. If someone came near him and drew a deep breath, he flinched before he could stop himself, and if a stranger looked like either of the men from the mugging he would shorten the conversation or leave altogether. Because he believed the event had happened because of the sort of person he was, every new brush with a crowd seemed to confirm that he was the kind of man bad things happened to. He became increasingly watchful in the chapel itself, unsettled by visitors standing too close in the aisle or by bereaved relatives breathing heavily in the waiting room, and the work that had once given him a steady sense of purpose started to feel like another place where danger might appear.

As Ravi pulled back from the parts of his life that placed him near strangers, the images returned with even more force. A face in a crowd, a rough exhale behind him, the smell of sweat in a cramped corridor could call up the robbery in an instant, and with the image came the same flash of rage and the same self-accusation. He found himself thinking that he should have handled it differently, that his fear had somehow made him smaller, and that other men would have escaped or fought back. Those thoughts made him watch even harder for danger, and the more he watched, the more often ordinary moments were swallowed by the old scene. Over time he was sleeping badly, arriving at work already tense, and arranging his day around avoiding the streets and public places where he might be confronted by breathing, bodies, or someone who looked related to the event. His wife had died the year before, and the loneliness of coming home to an empty apartment made the evenings especially hard; there was no one there to interrupt the images when they came. What finally brought Ravi in was the realization that he was beginning to fear not only the crowded city outside but also his own mind, because every reminder of the mugging seemed to drag him back into the conviction that he was helpless and exposed. He hoped for relief, but what frightened him most was that the next crowded room, the next heavy breath, would prove that he still could not keep bad things from happening to him.
